articles.title: I Rebuilt a CRM 3 Times Because I Solved the Wrong Problem
articles.excerpt: The first time I built this CRM, I thought I understood the problem. I knew how to build forms, connect database tables, create features, and import data. I was a developer. I knew how software was su…
articles.body: The first time I built this CRM, I thought I understood the problem. I knew how to build forms, connect database tables, create features, and import data. I was a developer. I knew how software was supposed to work. But I had overlooked something important: knowing how to build software isn't the same as understanding the problem you're solving. I ended up rebuilding the CRM three times before I got the solution right. And the biggest lesson had very little to do with writing code. I built it for developers, not users The CRM was built for an agency whose employees weren't necessarily technical. My first mistake was designing the application around what I thought people would naturally understand. If a field was labelled Email , I expected users to enter an email address.

articles.title: The 8am problem: what breaks when an agent has to keep an appointment
articles.excerpt: Ask someone what their AI product does while they are asleep and you usually get the same answer: it keeps running. Which is true, and also where the interesting part starts, because "keeps running" i…
articles.body: Ask someone what their AI product does while they are asleep and you usually get the same answer: it keeps running. Which is true, and also where the interesting part starts, because "keeps running" is not the hard bit. The hard bit is that it promised. A reminder fires or it doesn't; nobody dwells on it. A brief is different. If you told a tool that you want the thing waiting for you at eight, then eight is an appointment. A late brief is not a slow brief. It's a missed one, and you notice, because you were holding a coffee and a minute of attention open for it. I've argued before that a schedule is not a feature bolted onto an agent, it is the interface.

articles.title: Bench Triage: How to Trace Shorted Motherboard Power Rails with a Multimeter
articles.excerpt: When a laptop or desktop motherboard lands on the diagnostic bench with a "completely dead / no power" symptom, the instinct of novice repairers is often to plug in a power supply and start hunting fo…
articles.body: When a laptop or desktop motherboard lands on the diagnostic bench with a "completely dead / no power" symptom, the instinct of novice repairers is often to plug in a power supply and start hunting for warm chips with their fingertips or an isopropyl alcohol mist. In component-level engineering, that approach is a gamble that risks turning a simple capacitor failure into an unrecoverable crater in a $400 CPU or GPU die. Before any live voltage is introduced to an unverified board, bench protocol mandates a rigorous cold resistance triage . In this guide, we break down the exact systematic procedure used at our repair bench to trace shorted power rails, isolate defective MLCCs (multi-layer ceramic capacitors), and protect sensitive silicon using nothing more than a digital multimeter.
